AIDS bomb 
 *261.   SHRI RAVI SHANKAR PRASAD:              
SHRI B.J. PANDA: 
Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the US health authorities and CIA have warned 
India that it is a fast ticking AIDS bomb which would wreak havoc and weaken 
the economy; 
(b) whether India is now the most AIDS infected country in Asia; and 
(c) if so, the status of this disease in our country and the action plan to 
control this menace? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. 
ANBUMANI RAMADOSS): (a) The report of the National Intelligence Council 
(NIC) in USA states that the number of people living with HIV/AIDS will 
grow significantly by the end of th e decade and approximately 20-25 million 
Indians are likely to be infected (with HIV) by 2010. 
The National AIDS Control Organization, Government of India conducts 
2 

[23 July, 2004] RAJYA SABHA 
nationwide HIV Sentinel Surveillance every year during the period of August-
October. This data is also used to estimate the burden of HIV infections in the 
country in the adult population between 15-49 years of age group by taking 
certain assumptions into consideration. Based on the sentinel surveillance data 
2003, estimate of 5.1 million HIV infections was made. As such, we do not agree 
with National Intelligence Council (NIC) report of the USA. 
(b) India is not the most HIV infected country in Asia in terms of 
percentage of population infected with HIV. The prevalence of of HIV/AIDS in 
India is 0.96% among the general adult population, while HIV prevalence is 2% in 
Myanmar, 1.5% in Thailand and 2.6% in Cambodia, as indicated in UNAIDS 
country level progress Report, 2003. However, on account of our large 
population, a 0.9% prevalence translates into 5.1 million HIV infections. 
(c) The Action Plan being implemented to prevent and contain the 
spread of HIV/AIDS is as follows:— 
i. During the year 2002, a Parliamentary Forum on AIDS was set up and in 
July, 2003, this Parliamentary Forum on AIDS convened its first National 
Convention. This was a unique event. The National Convention was 
inaugurated by the Hon'ble Prime Minister and addressed by the 
Leader of opposition, Speaker of Lok Sabha, Deputy Prime Minister, 
Deputy Chairman of Rajya Sabha and other dignitaries. Elected 
representatives from three tiers of our parliamentary democracy 
across the political spectrum, from central, state and village panchayat 
levels came together to pledge their commitment to combat HIV/AIDS. 
Political advocacy is an important component of the National AIDS 
control programme. We propose to involve Members of Parliament 
more directly, at state level. 
ii. Extensive programme on awareness generation is being undertaken 
for the general population through multiple Channels. Health messages 
reach out through over 60,000 schools, 176 universities and 8000 
institutions via the School AIDS Education Programme and the 
University Talk AIDS Programme. Additionally, out of school youth are 
reached through the Village Talk AIDS Programme covering 385 
districts. The Family Health Awareness

rural areas across 550 districts, with behaviour change 
communication and management of STI clinics 
iii. Targetted interventions are being implemented at 933 high risk sites. 
iv. NACO supports 1020 blood banks, and 80 blood component 
separation units have been established. 
v. Services for Voluntary Counseling and Testing are being supported 
through 709 centres. 
vi. Services for prevention of HIV transmission from parent to child have 
been provided in the 291 antenatal clinics, at district hospitals and medical

vii. Free treatment is being provided for sexually transmitted infections

x. Training of medical and para-medical staff is being implemented, and

xi. Free anti-retroviral treatment has commenced from 1 st April, 2004, in 8 
hospitals of the 6 high prevalence states and NCT of Delhi. 
Government is committed to extending anti-retroviral treatment to over 
1,00,000 persons living with AIDS. We have already mobilized additional 
resources for this scaling up of treatment for AIDS, from the Global 
Fund on AIDS, TB and Malaria. 
xii. 51 Community Care Centres & 18 Drop in Centres have been 
established for care and support of AIDS cases. 
xiii. NACO had also facilitated the involvement of diverse sectors such as

Use of Alternative Medicines 
*265. SHRI R.R GOENKA: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY 
WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government's attention has been drawn to a recent warning of the 
World Health Organisation highlighting inter-alia increasing reports of adverse 
and even fatal reactions to the unregulat ed and often unsafe use of alternative 
medicines, ranging from acupuncture to herbal medicines and food supplements 
across the world; and 
(b) if so, the details of steps taken/bein g taken to regulate the practice of 
alternative systems of medicine and also for mass awareness to the dangers of 
over-the-counter purchase of such medicines and use of natural medicines, without 
consulting the physicians? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. ANBUMANl 
RAMADOSS): (a) and (b) Yes, Sir. A news-item appeared on 23rd June. 2004, 
in "Indian Express" wherein some observations attributed to WHO were made 
about adverse reactions of acupuncture, herbal medicines and food supplements etc. 
WHO, in its Press release dated 22nd June, 2004, have reported that adverse drug 
reactions to alternative medicines have more than doubled in the last three years. 
WHO has expressed its support for traditional and alternative medicines when 
these have demonstrated benefits for the patients and minimal risks. However, 
there have been many cases of consumers unknowingly using suspect or 
counterfeit products; choosing inappropriate therapies in self care as well as 
several reports of unintentional overdose. 
Various organizations have requested for recognition to various 
'unrecognised' streams of alternative systems of medicines particularly 
electrohomeopathy system of medicines. In order to look into their claims and 
also to examine the feasibility of making a legislation as per the directions 
issued by the Hon'ble Delhi High Court in its order dated 19.11.1998 in CWP 
No. 4015/96 and OA No. 8468/97, a Standing Committee of experts had been 
constituted under the Chairmanship of Director General, Indian Council of 
Medical Research (ICMR) vide this Ministry's Order dated 25th November, 2002, 
the Committee made in depth analysis of different schemes of alternative medicines 
including electropathy but has not recommended recognition to any of these 
alternative medicines 
7 

RAJYA SABHA [23 July, 2004] 
except the already recognized traditional systems of medicines namely 
Ayurveda, Siddha, Unani, Homoeopathy and drug less therapies such as Yoga 
and Naturopathy which were found to fulfill the essential and desirable criteria 
developed by the Committee. The recommendations of the Comm ittee have 
been examined and accepted by the Government. 
Indian Medicine Central Council (IMCC) Act of 1970, regulates the 
practice of Ayurveda, Siddha and Unan i doctors, teaching standards, medical 
ethics etc. The practice of Homoeopathy is regulated under the Central Council 
of Homoeopathy Act, 1973. The Drugs & Cosmetics Act, 1940, and rules 
thereunder regulate the quality standards of Ayurveda, Siddha, Unani and 
Homoeopathy drugs. Pharmacopoeial standards of 324 Ayurvedic and 45 Unani 
drugs have been published by the Government of India. It is necessary for the 
manufacturers to comply with these standards. 
Prices of Steel 
*266. SHRI PYARELAL KHANDELWAL: Will the Minister of STEEL 
be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that existing mechanism has not been able to check 
the prices of steel; 
(b) whether fluctuation in steel prices has created chaos in market during 
the previous year; 
(c) if so, the reasons behind such fluctuation of steel prices; and 
(d) the steps Government propose to take to check the prices of steel? 
THE MINISTER OF STEEL (SHRI RAM VILAS PASWAN): (a) In a 
liberalised and deregulated environment steel prices are determined by the 
interplay of market forces and the Government does not intervene directly to 
influence prices. Though the Government has tried to stabilise steel prices 
through various policy initiatives, domestic prices of steel have generally 
moved in tandem with international prices. 
(b) Concerns against rising steel prices have continuously been 
expressed by the Steel consuming industry throughout the previous year 
(c) While domestic prices are generally fagged with international prices, 
the price rise during the previous year is reported to be the result of rising 
8 

[23 July, 2004] RAJYA SABHA 
raw material costs during this period and growing demand. In a competitive market, 
steel producers adjust their prices depending on market conditions. 
(d) In a liberalised environment the Government does not intervene directly 
in the market to influence prices. However, the Government, through its policy 
initiatives, has taken several steps to ensure availability of steel and stablise the 
price in the domestic market which inter-alia include the following:- 
(i) reduction in customs duty on non alloy steel from 25% to 10% 
(ii) reduction in customs duty on alloy steel from 25% to 15%. 
(Hi) abolition of 4% Special Additional Duty (SAD) on imports. 
(iv) lowering of excise duty on steel items from 16% to 12% 
(v) substantial increase in the allocation of steel items, during 2004-05, for 
supply to the SSI units under the Small Scale Industries Corporations 
(SSIC) scheme. 
The Government is carefully monitoring the price situation and all 
necessary steps will be taken to help ensure stability in prices in the future.

Condition of Blood for Blood 
†*268. SHRIMATI SAVITA SHARDA: Will the Minister of HEALTH 
AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware that a large number of patients are dying 
in the country because of the condition of giving blood for blood; 
(b) if so, whether Government would consider not to apply this condition of 
giving blood for blood in the cases of serious patients in order to save their 
lives; and 
(c) the units of blood required every month in Delhi together with the total 
quantum of blood collected through the blood donation camps? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. ANBUMANI 
RAMADOSS): (a) to (c) Blood is an essential component of the body which 
provides sustenance to life Blood cannot be manufactured in a factory. It can 
only be collected from a human being an d transfused to those in need. Blood 
can be collected either from a voluntary, replacement or professional donor. The 
practice of professional blood donation has been banned in India from 1st 
January, 1998, subsequent to the Supreme Court judgement on this issue. 
Presently, the requirement of blood is met by a voluntary or a replacement 
donor. Since there is almost always a shortage of blood from voluntary blood 
donors, blood banks often insist 
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
11 

RAJYA SABHA [23 July, 2004] 
on releasing blood to a patient only after it is replaced by a relative or friend 
of the patient. This is known as a replacement donation. 
Legally, it is not mandatory that the blood given to a patient has to be 
replaced, nor is there any guidelines to this effect. The practice of asking for a 
replacement blood unit for a unit of blood released essentially seeks to make up 
the shortfall in blood stocks in the blood banks. In emergencies, blood is always 
released without insisting on replacement and the blood banks later make up 
through either replacement or voluntary collections. It would be incorrect to state 
that patients are dying due to the system of replacement donations. 
As regards the requirement of blood units for Delhi, it varies according to 
seasons and incidence of various diseases. The estimated average annual 
requirement for Delhi is about 3.00 lakh units of blood. Delhi has reported an 
annual blood collection of 3,26,861 units during the year 2003. 76,644 of this 
(23.4%) was from voluntary blood donation and the rest was collected from 
replacement donors. It is estimated that 25% of the total blood collection in 
Delhi is separated into blood components.

(b) if so, the details in this regard with allocation proposed to be made for the 
programme; and 
(c) the areas identified for accentuated healthcare focus? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. 
ANBUMANI RAMADOSS): (a) to (c) Gove rnment has been taking various 
steps to improve healthcare facilities, especially in the rural areas of the country. 
In order to improve primary health care, the National Health Policy, 2002, 
envisages to increase sectoral outlays in the primary sector from around 48% to 
55%. The Common Minimum Programme of the Government envisages raising 
the public spending on Health to at 2-3% of GDP over the next 5 years, with 
focus on primary health care. 
Healthcare in the rural areas is provided through a network of 1,45,980 Sub-
Centres, 22842 Primary Health Care Centres (PHCs) and 3043 Community 
Health Centres (CHCs). A Sub-Centre is the most peripheral contact point 
between the health care system and the community. A Sub-centre is set up for 
every 5,000 population in the rural areas, and for every 3,000 population in desert, 
hilly and tribal areas. A PHC is a referral unit for six sub-centres, and a CHC is a 
30-bedded hospital/referral unit for 4 PHCs with specialized services. 
A wide range of services is delivered through this country-wide network. These 
relate to the areas of maternal health, child health including immunization, 
and training of service providers and health functionaries. The Government of 
India also has schemes for strengthening the primary health infrastructure and 
services through provision of financial assistance for salaries and civil works, 
supply of drugs and vaccines and provision of delivery kits. 
A table indicating the budgetary outlay for the Department of Family 
Welfare's schemes aimed at the rural population is given in the Statement-I (See 
below)

Spurious Medicines 
*277. SHRIMATI VANGA GEETHA: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether spurious and counterfeit medicines are prevalent in the market 
in an alarming proportion; 
(b) if so, the reasons for not checking entry of such medicines; and 
27 

RAJYA SABHA [23 July, 2004] 
(c) the remedial measures proposed to check the menace effectively and 
uniformally throughout the country? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. 
ANBUMANI RAMADOSS): (a) to (e) The term 'Spurious Drug' has been 
defined under Section 17-B of the Drug and Cosmetics Act, 1940, as amended by 
the Drugs and Cosmetics (Amendment) Act, 1982. In brief, a drug shall be 
deemed to be spurious if it is manufactured under a name which belongs to 
another drug, if it is an imitation of another drug or if it has been substituted 
wholly or partly by another drug or if it wrongly claims to be the product of 
another manufacturer. 
There is no definition for "counterfeit" drugs under the Drugs and 
Cosmetics Act, 1940. Adrug is popularly termed as 'fake' or counterfeit* by the 
media when it is maerially copied from a leader brand. 
There have been media reports quoting varying figures anywhere from 0.5% 
to 35% about the alleged extent of circulation of spurious drugs in the country. 
However, as per the feedback availa ble from the Drugs Controllers of 
States/UTs, 36924,38824,36314,39465 drug samples were tested during the 
period 2000-01, 2001-02, 2002-03 and 2003-04 out of which 112, 96, 125 and 
108 samples respectively were found spurious which is 0.3,0.25,0.34 and 0.27 
percent of the samples reported spurious whereas for the last three years around 
10% of the samples tested were found to be not of standard quality. Thus, it does 
not appear that spurious and counterfeit medicines are prevalent in the market 
in alarming proportions. However, the Government had taken a serious note of 
such reports and constituted an expert  committee under the Chairmanship of 
Dr. R.A. Mashelkar in January, 2003 to undertake a comprehensive 
examination of drug regulatory issues including spurious drugs in the 
country. 
Based on the recommendations of Dr. R.A. Mashelkar Committee, a 
legislation to amend the penal provisions of Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940, 
and to provide for stricter penalties to the offenders including a maximum 
penalty of capital punishment, was introduced in the Parliament in December, 
2003. 
The salient amendments proposed under the Bill are given below:— 
1.  Enhance the punishments relating to spurious or adulterated drugs 
28 

[23 July, 2004] RAJYA SABHA 
leading to death or grievous hurt within the meaning of Section 320 
IPC upto punishment of death or imprisonment for a term which 
shall not be less than 10 years but which may extend to imprisonment 
for life and shall also be liable to fine of one lakh rupees or upto three 
times the value of the goods seized, whichever is higher. 
2. Penalties for subsequent offences to be enhanced upto 10 years and with 
fine which shall not be less than one lakh rupees. 
3. Offences relating to spurious or adulterated drugs to be made non-
bailable and cognizable. 
4. Provision for setting up of special courts to try offences of spurious or 
adulterated drugs. 
5. To confer powers upon police offecers not below the rank of sub-
inspector or other designated officer to institute prosecutions under the 
said Act. 
6. Provision for compounding of offences for minor offences under the 
Act. 
The proposed amendments will make the law deterrent to the offenders involved 
in the manufacture or sale of spurious drugs. The involvement of enforcing 
agencies like Police will help in speedy investigations to book the culprits and 
in controlling anti-social elements involved in such activities. 
Since the Bill has now lapsed with the dissolution of previous Lok Sabha, 
necessary action to introduce a bill to enhance penalties for manufacture 
and/or sale of spurious and/or adulterated drugs under the Drugs & Cosmetics 
Act, 1940, will be initiated by the Ministry of Health & Family Welfare.

(1) There is no link established between use of Endosulfan in Plantation 
Corporation of Kerala (PCK) pl antations and health problems 
reported in Padre village. 
(2) In consideration of the recommendations given by various other 
committees, the Committee recommende d that aerial spraying of 
pesticides may not be allowed at all in any situations including in PCK 
plantations to ensure full safety. 
46 

[23 July, 2004] RAJYA SABHA 
(3) The application of all pesticides including Endosulfan is to be done 
adhering to regulatory stipulations in force from time to time. 
(4) The pesticides manufacturers should take necessary steps to promote 
and educate sellers and users to ensure correct and safe use of all 
pesticides. 
(5) Since India has adequate pre-registration data requirement and post-
registration review processes concerning use of pesticides, the 
Committee recommended that scie nce-based responses be made 
available to all stake-holders and general public by registration 
authorities. There is often a huge gap between perception of the risk 
and actual scientific risk assessment. This gap is to be filled by proper 
and timely propagation of knowledge and information. 
(6) Since the relationship of alleged illness with Endosulfan in Padre could 
not be established, the Committee recommended to conduct a 
comprehensive, well designed and detailed health and 
epidemiological study in the entire cashew plantation area of Kerala to 
ascertain the incidences of diseases in Padre vis-a-vis Kerala State 
averages and in case there is evid ence of unusual health problem to 
investigate and if possible pinpoint the probable/most probable factor(s) 
that are responsible for alleged health problems. 
(7) Finally, after considering all above factors and available reports, the 
Committee recommended that use of Endosulfan be continued as per 
provisions of Insecticides Act, 1968. 
 
(c) Dubey Committee Report was based on the examination of the report 
of National Institute of Occupational Health, Kerala Agriculture University, 
Fredrick Institute of Plant Protection and Toxicology (FIPPAT), now 
International Institute of Biotechnology and Toxicology (IIBT), Dr. 
Achyuthan Committee, information received from District Medical Officer, 
Kasargod, State Agriculture Universities, Indian Council of Agricultural 
Research Institutes, field visits, deliberations and inputs from members and 
experts. 
(d) and (e) The report of IIBT reveals existence/presence of peaks of

Endosulfan, Beta Endosulfan and Endosulfan Sulphate in 5 out of the 112

Demand of fertilizers 
1062. SHRI BALAWANT ALIAS BAL APTE: Will the Minister of 
CHEMICALS AND FERTILIZERS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the dema nd of chemical fertilizers in the 
country is met with domestic production; 
(b) if not, the percentage of average annual demand met by imported 
fertilizers; 
(c) whether Government have fixed any target for marking the country self-
dependent in respect of fertilizers; and 
(d) if so, the time-limit fixed for achieving the target? 
THE MINISTER OF CHEMICALS AND FERTILIZERS (SHRI RAM 
VILAS PASWAN). (a) The country is near ly self-sufficient in meeting the 
demand of nitrogenous and phosphatic fertilizers, namely Urea, DAP and NPK 
complexes. Whenever there is a gap in demand-supply situation of urea, the 
Government imports urea through State Trading Enterprises (STEs). As regard 
DAP, being a de-controlled and de-canalized fertilizer, its import depends on 
prevailing international prices and the domestic market demand-supply situation 
in the country. As regard MOP, the country 
73 

RAJYA SABHA [23 July, 2004] 
is dependent on total imports in the absence of any exploitable reserves of potash in 
the country. 
(b) There was no import of urea during the last two years. However, in case of 
DAP, the percentage of demand met by import during 2002-03 and 2003-04. 
(c) and (d) The Government has been pursuing policies which are 
conducive for encouraging investment in fertilizer sector so as to achieve self-
sufficiency in meeting the indigenous requirement of major fertilizers. In case of 
urea, the Government has recently announced the pricing policy for investment to 
be made in (a) new and expansion projects of urea and (b) existing non-gas 
based urea units converting to natural gas/LNG for feedstock/fuel. In Order to 
augment indigenous availability of urea, IFFCO and KRIBHCO the multi-state 
cooperative societies, are setting up a joint venture in Sur, Oman with Oman oil 
Company and the entire production of 16.52 lakh MT of urea will be bought by 
the Government. On the other hand, installed capacity (54.20 lakh MT in 
nutrient terms) of phosphatic fertilizers is sufficient enough to meet the 
current level of requirement (average consumption of 46-47 lakh MT of last 
three years).

1083. PROF. SAIF-UD-DIN SOZ: Will the Minister of ENVIRONMENT 
AND FORESTS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact the Government had made public a white paper on tackling 
pollution in Delhi in the year 1997-98; and 
(b) if so, the action taken in respect of the decisions Government had announced? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF ENVIRONMENT 
97 

RAJYA SABHA [23 July, 2004] 
AND FORESTS (SHRI NAMO NARAIN MEENA): (a) Yes, Sir. The 
Government has brought out a White Paper on Pollution in Delhi with an Action 
Plan for the prevention and control of pollution in the National Capital Region of 
Delhi during 1997-98. It contained action plan corresponding to issues such as air 
pollution with specific reference to vehicular pollution, water pollution, solid 
waste management, industrial pollution and noise "pollution. It also included 
setting up of Sewage Treatment Plants (STPs) and Common Effluent Treatment 
Plants (CETPs) for treatment of waste water from the human settlement as well 
as the industries. 
(b) The Government has taken several actions to curb the pollution in Delhi, 
which include:— 
* Improvement in fuel quality. 
* Measures to control fuel adulteration. 
* Improvement in vehicular technology. 
* Conversion of vehicle fleet, i.e. buses, autos, taxis to Compressed Natural 
Gas (CNG) mode. 
* Use of beneficiated coal in thermal power plant stations. 
* Closure of brick kilns, hot-mix plants and stone crushers in National 
Capital Territory of Delhi. 
* Source specific noise standards for generator sets, fire crackers and 
other industries have been notified to curb noise pollution. 
* Augmentation of sewage treatment capacity and capacity utilisation. 
* Three STPs have been installed under the Yamuna Action Plan Phase I 
which help to treat municipal waste water. 
* Bio-medical Wastes (Management & Handling) Rules and Rules for 
Flyash Utilization have been notified. 
* 1328 hazardous and noxious industries have been closed by the order of 
Hon'ble Supreme Court.

1097. SHRIMATI N.P. DURGA: W ill the Minister of HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware that recently a German based 
European Molecular Biology Laboratory, Heidelberg, has identified four 
proteins that affect the ability of malaria parasite to survive in mosquitoes; and 
(b) if so, the results of the research? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRIMATI PANABAKA LAKSHMI): (a) and (b) Yes, 
Sir. Scientists at European Molocular Biology Laboratory (EMBL), 
120 

[23 July, 2004] RAJYA SABHA 
Heidelberg are reported to have identified four mosquito proteins that affect the 
ability of malaria parasite (Plasmodium) to survive and develop in the malaria 
carrier mosquito (Anopheles). 
Two of the mosquito proteins i.e. TEP1 and LRIM1 have been shown to be 
defendors of the mosquito killing of the parasite in insect's gut and by 
enhancing these natural defenders, parasite mosquito cycle can be blocked. 
In addition to defender proteins, two other proteins CTL4 and CTLMA2 have 
been discovered, which have an opposite effect, actually protecting the parasite 
as it develops in the mosquito gut. If these proteins were eliminated, the 
parasite died. 
This breakthrough in research could be used to block the transmission of 
malaria parasite from mosquito to man.

laboratory practices norms for mandatory accreditation for health care labs in 
the country under the National Bureau for Accreditation of Laboratories; and

THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. 
ANBUMANI RAMADOSS): (a) to (c) The recommendations in respect of a 
Centralized Drug Regulatory system in the country to deal with technical legal 
and laboratory related aspects of the Drugs sector and that accreditation with 
National Accreditation Board for Laboratories (NABL) should be made 
mandatory for all drug testing Labs, including Government Labs, were made by a

competent and trained manpower and with adequate budget.

Laboratory Practices (GLP) norms as statutory requirement for 
approved testing laboratories and also the in-house testing 
laboratories of the manufacturers.

laboratories including Government Laboratories. 
(5) The State testing laboratories should be frequently audited by a team 
of experts to ensure their proper functioning.

Strengthening Railway Bridges 
1127. SHRI R. K. ANAND: Will the Minister of RAILWAYS be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that a large nu mber of existing railway bridges are 
between 80 to 100 years old and were constructed to handle only lighter 
standard of loading than prevalent, i.e. there has been tremendous growth of load 
both in freight as well as passenger traffic since the construction of these 
bridges; 
(b) if so, the steps taken to strengthen the existing railway bridges to handle 
heavier load of freight and passengers; and 
(c) the steps taken to replace these railway bridges? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RAILWAYS 
(SHRI R. VELU): (a) It is a fact that about 75600 bridges out of 1,19,984 
bridges are between 80 to 100 years old and were constructed to handle loading 
prevalent at the time of their construction. 
(b) and(c) In case of introduction of heavier axle load in a particular 
section, thorough study is carried out for suitability of existing bridges. If 
required, bridges are rehabilitated/rebuilt to bear the heavier axle load of 
freight/passenger trains. 
145 

RAJYA SABHA [23 July, 2004] 
Repair & Rehabilitation of old railway bridges is a continuous process. A well 
laid down system of multi-tier inspection of bridges is followed in the Indian 
Railways. The rehabilitation/rebuilding of the bridges is carried out based on the 
physical condition as ascertained during inspection and not on the basis of age 
alone. In case a section is selected for introduction of heavier loads, all the bridges of 
that section are reviewed and strengthened as per requirement.

Rail Tracks 
†1131. SHRI ISAM SINGH: Will the Minister of RAILWAYS be pleased 
to state: 
(a) whether the rail tracks in our country are as per the specifications of 
modern latest engine manufactured; and 
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
147 

RAJYA SABHA [23 July, 2004] 
(b) if not, the action plan of Government to deal with it? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RAILWAYS 
(SHRI R. VELU): (a) and (b) Modern latest engines are expected to be 
deployed on certain selected sections only as per needs. However, even on such 
selected sections, the infrastructure e.g. Track, Bridges, Signals and 
Telecommunication etc., may need major upgradation, if full potential of these 
modern latest engines, is to be realized. 
Such upgradation, is a costly activity and is normally planned and 
executed at a time when infrastructure replacement works are undertaken next. 
Such replacements are on age-cum-condition basis and their execution 
depends upon availability of funds. However, whenever such replacements are 
undertaken, modern infrastructure, as per route classification and annual 
traffic density etc. is adopted. 
Till such time, required infrastructure is available, the rolling stocks, e.g. 
engines, wagons etc., including the modern latest engines, are allowed to be run at 
such maximum speeds and under such conditions, as are considered safe for 
the available infrastructure including track.

1145. SHRI R. P. GOENKA: will the Minister of RAILWAYS be pleased to

(a) whether it is a fact that the Asian Development Bank (ADB) has 
agreed to invest about one billion do llars in the Indian Railway system

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RAILWAYS 
(SHRI R VELU): (a) Asian Development Bank (ADB) has agreed to extend an 
assistance for the railway sector in 3 phases, with the quantum in the first 2 
phases amounting to around US dollar 600 million. The objective of the 
assistance is to improve the performance of the sector by (i) financing priority 
investments to overcome railway capacity bottlenecks and improve operational 
efficiency/safety and (ii) supporting implementation of a program of reforms 
formulated by the Ministry of Railway s (MOR) to improve Indian Railway's 
commercial orientation. In Phase-I, a loan amount of US Dollar 313.6 million has 
been approved. Subsequent phases of the loan are linked to the implementation of 
MOR's reform programme over the period from 2002 to 2010.

Consultant by ADB under a Technical Assistance (TA) grant, outside the loan, 
for providing Management Consulting Services to Ministry of Railways. The 
objective of the TA is to study (i) business development and business opportunities 
and (ii) progress of implementation of the reform programme. 
The components of the reform programme formulated by MOR and 
accepted by ADB are as under:

Accountability on Safety Issues 
1157. SHRIMATI SARLA MAHESHWARI: Will the Minister of 
RAILWAYS be pleased to state: 
(a) why does the Commissioner of Rail Safety probe accidents with an air 
of secrecy and delays the submission of its report; 
(b) whether the lack of accountability of the Railways on the issue of safety 
needs to be urgently addressed; and 
(c) if so, the steps Government propose to take in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RAILWAYS 
(SHRI R. VELU): (a) The statutory inquiries into the accidents by the 
Commissioner of Railway Safety are held after notifying date, time and venue 
in the press inviting persons having any information to give evidence. Preliminary 
reports are given within 10-15 days including provisional findings which are 
released to the Press. This is followed by a detailed report in about three 
months. 
(b) and (c) Safety is given paramount importance on Indian Railways and 
every effort is made to prevent accide nts. Acts of omission and Commission, 
if any, on the part of railway staff are taken up and responsibility fixed for 
lapses not only resulting into accidents but also detected during routine 
checks and inspections.
